trial_name: FACTT — Pulmonary-Artery vs Central Venous Catheter in Acute Lung Injury (2006)
citation: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) Clinical Trials Network. Pulmonary-artery versus central venous catheter to guide treatment of acute lung injury. N Engl J Med. 2006;354(21):2213-2224
one_liner: In early acute lung injury, pulmonary-artery catheter-guided protocolised management did not improve survival or ventilator-free days compared with central venous catheter-guided management, and was associated with more complications, particularly arrhythmias.

pico.population: Mechanically ventilated adults with acute lung injury (PaO2/FiO2 ≤300, bilateral infiltrates, no left atrial hypertension) enrolled within 48 hours of meeting criteria.
pico.intervention: Pulmonary-artery catheter insertion with protocolised haemodynamic management using PAC-derived measures (PAOP, cardiac index) to guide fluids, diuretics, vasopressors, inotropes.
pico.comparison: Central venous catheter insertion with protocolised haemodynamic management using CVP-based targets.
pico.outcome: Death before hospital discharge home within 60 days (primary); ventilator-free days, ICU-free days, catheter-related complications.

background.existing_knowledge: Pulmonary-artery catheterisation was widely used to estimate filling pressures, cardiac output, and mixed venous oxygenation to guide haemodynamic decisions, but prior evidence did not establish patient-centred benefit across heterogeneous ICU populations.
background.knowledge_gap: In acute lung injury, fluid and vasopressor decisions are frequent and high-stakes; it was unclear whether PAC-derived information improves outcomes compared with CVC-based monitoring when management is protocolised.
background.hypothesis: PAC-guided protocolised management would reduce death before hospital discharge home within 60 days compared with CVC-guided protocolised management.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, factorial trial (PAC vs CVC, and liberal vs conservative fluid strategy), open-label, protocol-driven.
methods.setting: Adult ICUs in ARDS Network participating hospitals (US and Canada).

inclusion: ALI criteria: bilateral infiltrates, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300, no clinical evidence of left atrial hypertension
Enrolled within 48 hours of meeting ALI criteria
exclusion: Pre-existing PAC after onset of ALI
Chronic conditions expected to confound survival or weaning (severe chronic cardiopulmonary, renal, neurological, hepatic, or neuromuscular disease)

methods.intervention: Pulmonary-artery catheter insertion (targeted within 4 hours of randomisation). Protocolised haemodynamic management using PAC-derived measures (PAOP, cardiac index) to drive fluid/diuretic/vasopressor/inotrope instructions. Concurrent randomisation to liberal or conservative fluid strategy.
methods.comparison: Central venous catheter insertion (targeted within 4 hours). Protocolised management using CVP-based targets with same clinical protocol framework. Concurrent randomisation to same fluid strategy.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (catheter type inherently difficult to blind); primary and key secondary outcomes were objective.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned sample size ~1000 to detect a 10 percentage point reduction in primary endpoint with 90% power at 5% two-sided significance.
methods.primary_outcome: Death before hospital discharge home within 60 days.
methods.follow_up: Primary endpoint through 60 days; morbidity outcomes through day 28; in-hospital safety outcomes.

headline_bullets: No difference in 60-day mortality: 27.4% PAC vs 26.3% CVC (absolute difference 1.1%, 95% CI −4.4 to 6.6; P=0.69)
Ventilator-free days and ICU-free days were similar (13.2 vs 13.5, P=0.58; 12.0 vs 12.5, P=0.40)
Catheter-related complications were higher with PAC (19% vs 9%, P<0.001), driven by arrhythmias requiring treatment (12% vs 0.2%, P<0.001)
No interaction between catheter type and fluid strategy for primary endpoint (P=0.39)

outcomes_table.outcome: Death before hospital discharge home within 60 days

outcomes_table.note: Composite of mechanical, arrhythmic, infectious, thrombotic
Dominant driver of excess complications with PAC
Mechanical complication; higher absolute count in CVC arm

outcomes_table.outcome: Packed red-cell transfusion during study period
outcomes_table.note: Potential signal of differential procedural/bleeding practice or illness trajectory

outcomes_table.outcome: Positive blood cultures during catheter period

subgroup_table.note: No differential benefit reported; effect estimates not provided in manuscript
No interaction between catheter type and fluid strategy for primary endpoint

safety: Any catheter-related complication: PAC 19% vs CVC 9% (P<0.001)
Arrhythmia requiring treatment: PAC 12% vs CVC 0.2% (P<0.001)
Packed red-cell transfusion: PAC 38% vs CVC 30% (P=0.008)
Positive blood cultures during catheter period: PAC 14.2% vs CVC 9.4% (P=0.02)
Kidney replacement therapy: PAC 14% vs CVC 11% (P=0.15)

domains.notes: Central, protocolised randomisation with stratification by hospital and fluid strategy; allocation concealment not detailed beyond central assignment.
Unblinded intervention; primary and key secondary endpoints were objective, reducing detection bias.
1001 randomised; loss to follow-up for primary endpoint not reported; ITT analysis.
High protocol adherence (91 ± 1% PAC vs 88 ± 1% CVC; P=0.12); low crossover (4 PAC→CVC, 5 CVC→PAC).
Groups similar on age, APACHE III, PaO2/FiO2, shock prevalence.
Crossover rare; management instructions differed modestly; dobutamine use higher in PAC (7% vs 2%, P<0.001) without outcome benefit.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity appears strong given central randomisation, very low crossover, high protocol adherence, and objective endpoints; main limitation is unavoidable lack of blinding with potential co-intervention effects.

domains.notes: Represents ventilated adults with early ALI in high-resource ICUs, enrolled within 48 hours; exclusions (prolonged ALI, pre-existing PAC, severe chronic diseases) narrow applicability.

Findings most applicable to ICUs with protocolised management and experienced staff; generalisation to resource-limited settings constrained; may not extend to niche populations (e.g., right ventricular failure) where PAC information is uniquely actionable.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is moderate: reflects early ALI/ARDS care in experienced, protocol-capable centres, but broader applicability limited by selective exclusions and protocolised nature of intervention.

strengths: Large, multicentre randomised evaluation (n=1001) with clinically meaningful primary endpoint.
Early enrolment (≤48 hours after ALI criteria met) and prespecified insertion window (≤4 hours) increased biological plausibility for benefit.
High protocol fidelity and low crossover (4 vs 5 patients) improve separation of monitoring strategy.
Factorial platform enabled explicit assessment for interaction with fluid strategy (interaction P=0.39).
limitations: Unblinded intervention introduces potential performance bias and co-intervention variability.
Protocolised management may attenuate incremental value of PAC-derived information compared with clinician-directed PAC use; trial estimates effect under protocol constraints.
Primary endpoint (death before discharge home by day 60) can be influenced by discharge practices, though balanced by randomisation.
Trial not designed to fully quantify extremely rare catastrophic PAC complications; however, clinically important arrhythmias were substantially more common with PAC (12% vs 0.2%).

critical_appraisal.summary: FACTT is a well-conducted, large RCT demonstrating no benefit of PAC-guided protocolised management over CVC-guided management in early ALI, with higher complication rates; the findings support avoiding routine PAC use in this population.
strengths: High protocol adherence and low crossover
weaknesses: Protocolised management may not reflect real-world PAC use
Primary endpoint influenced by discharge practices

sections.authors_conclusion: Routine PAC use in ALI did not improve patient-centred outcomes when compared with CVC-based targets within a protocolised management framework. The absence of benefit, coupled with higher complication rates, supports a default strategy of using less invasive monitoring unless a patient-specific indication exists.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In early acute lung injury, pulmonary-artery catheters should not be used routinely; central venous catheter-based monitoring is sufficient for protocolised haemodynamic management.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Mechanically ventilated adults with early ALI/ARDS in ICUs capable of protocolised fluid and vasopressor management.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: PACs are never useful; they may still have a role in selected patients with complex haemodynamic instability where specific PAC-derived data could alter management, but this trial does not support routine use.
implementation_caveats: Protocolised management was used; results may differ with clinician-directed PAC use
Complication rates may vary by operator experience and setting
The trial did not evaluate advanced haemodynamic monitoring devices (e.g., echocardiography, pulse contour analysis)

controversies.topic: Interpretation of what the trial truly tests
controversies.notes: Evaluates PAC-guided targets embedded in a rigid protocol versus CVP-guided targets, not discretionary clinician-directed PAC decision-making.
Arrhythmias requiring treatment occurred in 12% with PAC vs 0.2% with CVC (P<0.001), shifting risk–benefit against routine PAC placement even in expert centres.
Critical care has moved toward less invasive haemodynamic assessment (bedside echocardiography) and selective use of advanced monitoring, consistent with these data.
Other randomised evaluations and systematic syntheses have not established routine outcome benefit for PACs across ICU populations comparable to ALI/ARDS.

unresolved_questions: Whether PACs provide benefit in specific subgroups (e.g., right ventricular failure, severe shock) where haemodynamic data might uniquely guide therapy.
Optimal haemodynamic monitoring strategy in ARDS with concomitant shock.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In early ALI, PAC-guided protocolised management does not improve outcomes over CVC-guided management and causes more arrhythmias; avoid routine PAC use.
